chapter_theme: Akananuru 181 to 200 in the anthology's fixed cycle of lands: ten paalai poems in which men argue with their hearts about going for wealth, three of them giving up the journey, and mothers mourn eloped daughters; around them hill trysts ruled by the weather and the harvest, a marutham quarrel told by both courtesan and wife, waiting in the promised rains, and neythal disclosure and invitation. Puram names (Minjili and Eyinan, Pazhaiyan of Por, Thithiyan and Anni Minjili, Kannan Ezhini, Nannan and Narmudi Cheral) serve as measures for private feeling.

181.reading: A man on the road tells his heart, which cannot face the hard forest and wants to turn back, to go and report his state to the girl who lives on a great sand dune in a fragrant street of Pukar, a town of high walls, a Shiva shrine and a ford where women leave their dolls.
181.nuance: Most of the poem is the address of the girl's home, built up as a chain of places; the fall of Aay Eyinan to Minjili, with a flock of birds massing over the field and hiding the sun, is set beside the Kaveri's heaped white sand, so a battle memory becomes the measure of how thick that sand lies. The heart is not rebuked into going on, as in Akananuru 21; it is sent back as a messenger while the man goes forward.

thinai_evidence.note: a man mid-journey whose heart wants to turn back to the woman

comparisons.tenor: the Kaveri's sand, gathered and heaped into white dunes
Minjili's strength in battle

182.reading: The friend tells the man of the hill country, where the hunter drinks jackfruit toddy and kills a porcupine, that the girl weeps every night thinking of him coming alone through midnight storms that strike down snakes, so he must come by full daylight instead.
182.nuance: The opening hunter, who returns with his kill through bloodied grass, is the hill's ordinary daytime courage set against the man's lonely night journey; the closing slope strewn with alari petals is likened to the velan's ground of possession, a hint of the mother's suspicion that the friend does not voice.

thinai_evidence.note: hill hunters, vengai and jackfruit, and a night tryst

comparisons.tenor: the slope strewn with fallen alari petals where the stag leaps

183.reading: The woman tells her friend that she was promised he would not stay long, though he went far across the waste; now the rain clouds, having drunk the sea, have come up from the west like herds of she-elephants, the cold wind spreads the scent of opening pidavu buds, and she asks whether those who are parted do not suffer.
183.nuance: The season he named has arrived on time while he has not, so the clouds prove the friend's comfort false; the clouds are described as a herd of pregnant she-elephants gathering with their kin, a picture of fullness and company set against her solitude.

thinai_evidence.note: the heroine waits through the promised rains; the road is only mentioned

comparisons.tenor: the dark rain clouds appearing here and there
her eyes, dark and wet like the blue water lily

occasion.words: தலைமகன் குறித்த பருவவரவு கண்டு தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் குறித்த பருவவரவு கண்டு தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

184.reading: The friend greets the returning man: his coming at red dusk, his chariot bells ringing like a waterfall on rock, past fields where pidavu and jasmine bloom and the stag rests with its doe, is sweet not only to his wife, the light of the house who bore him a son, but to her too.
184.nuance: The friend's blessing 'may your life flourish' and her claim that the joy is hers as well make the welcome public; the wife is praised as mother and as 'light of the clan' before anything is said of her love, the karpu household seen from outside.

thinai_evidence.note: jasmine, pidavu, the scrub and the deer at evening with the hero returned

comparisons.tenor: the ringing of the chariot's many bells

iraicchi.act: the stag, having drunk clear water, stays at rest beside its spotted doe
iraicchi.sense: the man who has finished his hard work now stays with his wife, as the stag on his road stays with its doe

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் வினைவயிற்பிரிந்து வந்து எய்தியவிடத்து தோழி புல்லுமகிழ்வு உரைத்தது.

185.reading: The woman tells her friend that her bangles slip and her shoulders lose their beauty while her lover, as if his life were made of iron, has hardened himself and crossed the scorched summer hills where bamboo bursts like a warrior's bowstring and leafless ilavam blazes like the lamps of a great festival.
185.nuance: Her only accusation is the iron simile: he is not cruel but able, வலித்து வல்லினர, to will the parting, and that ability is what she cannot match; the festival lamps on the bare ilavam are a celebration seen from inside her loss.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer waste with failed rain and leafless ilavam

comparisons.tenor: her lover, who could steel himself to leave
the dry bamboo bursting with a crack
the leafless ilavam trees in full red flower

186.reading: The courtesan, speaking so that the wife's companions hear, says the gossip about her and the lord of the town is loud, though their bond was only a bathing friendship on a raft of reed; he is now with another woman, and if the wife quarrels with her, let her know that it is her own husband, who leaves women pale, that is the enemy living in her house.
186.nuance: The courtesan both disowns and boasts: he has never broken her bangles, which stand firm like Pazhaiyan's fort of Por, so she is not the one he leaves; the lotus leaf that flaps like an elephant's ear at every gust may be read as his fickleness, but the poem does not make the match itself.

thinai_evidence.note: lotus pond, reed raft and the lord of the town

comparisons.tenor: the broad lotus leaf swaying at each gust
her close-set bangles, which he has never broken
the wife's own husband

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks within the wife's hearing, to the heroine's companions (பாங்காயினார்), recorded as overhearer thozhi

187.reading: The woman asks her friend whether their sanded courtyard, lovely as the first day of a warrior festival, will grow lonely now that her lover, ashamed to prolong their hidden union, has gone for wealth to a far land, across hills where a sleeping elephant looks like a fishing boat at rest on the sea.
187.nuance: The union was hidden and long, and he leaves out of shame at its length (நாண் உடைமையின்) and with thoughts of 'our standing' (நம் உயர்வு): the journey is for the marriage that will end the secrecy. The road is drawn in detail, a deserted country emptied by raids and a hamlet that shelters guests at night.

thinai_evidence.note: summer forest drying and the hard road of the parting

comparisons.tenor: the bright sanded courtyard of their house
the forked bright young leaves of the yaa tree
the elephant asleep with its trunk curled under the dark hill

colophon.thurai: பிரிவுணர்த்தியதோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது. தலைமகன்பிரிவின்கண் தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

188.reading: The friend, at night and within the hidden lover's hearing, scolds the thundering, lightning-flashing cloud for raging to no purpose, and asks it whether it will also bring to an end the millet field the hill girl guards with her companions, wearing vengai flowers and scaring birds.
188.nuance: Addressing the cloud is a way of speaking to the man: the rain will ripen the millet, the harvest will end the guarding, and with it the day meetings, so he should act. The cloud's lightning is likened to the swords of just kings' warriors, a puram image used to scare a lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill girl guarding the millet with her rattle under vengai

comparisons.tenor: the thunder of the cloud
the flashes of lightning
the golden vengai flowers

189.reading: The foster mother laments that the little girl has gone off with the youth across the scorched hills, where a tusker clutching his mate breaks a path, and has become another's; she herself wanders bewildered at home, and the town, whose streets ring with music, has lost the thing it loved.
189.nuance: Her grief widens from herself to the town: the girl was the town's treasure, so the loss is public. The tusker that shelters its young mate and treads a path through the drought answers her fear with a picture of a guarded crossing; on our reading that is the sense the poem lets rise without saying it.

thinai_evidence.note: the parched summer road of an elopement

comparisons.tenor: the tusker lifting its trunk as it leads its mate

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she laments aloud

iraicchi.act: the tusker keeps his young she-elephant close and treads a track for her through the dry hills
iraicchi.sense: the youth who has taken the girl across the same land may guard and lead her as the tusker does its mate

190.reading: The friend tells the foster mother not to fret over the town's gossip about the girl and the lord of the shore: one evening, as the wind-driven sea beat the bay, a fierce shark struck in the estuary, he speared it, and with his tired horses he came and rested by them on the sand at dusk.
190.nuance: This is the friend's disclosure (அறத்தொடு நிற்றல): she presents the bond as born of a rescue at sea, which gives the family an honourable reason to accept him. The closing words சேர்ந்தன்றே இலனே are hard to construe, so who came to whom, and whether he stayed, is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: salt heaps, fishing boats, punnai and the seaside grove

191.reading: The man tells his heart that if, having gone, it plans to stay away for wealth across the hot road where the salt-carriers' bullock bells tell travellers they are safe, it should first be able to say firmly to the woman with soft hair like rippled sand that she will bear it.
191.nuance: He does not refuse the journey outright; he sets the heart a test it cannot pass, telling her to her face, and so gives up going. The bells of the salt-carriers, which reassure travellers, are the reassurance he cannot give her.

thinai_evidence.note: the long hot road of the wealth journey

comparisons.tenor: her spread-out black hair
the chain of bells on the salt-carriers' bullocks

192.reading: The friend tells the man of the high hills that the girl's moon-bright forehead has turned the colour of gold with longing; the millet has been reaped by parrots and junglefowl, and a snake-spat gem washed down by the falls lights up the village street, so if he comes at midnight she has lost even the night, and pity her.
192.nuance: Each detail closes a way: the end of the harvest ends her days in the field, and the street lit by the gem ends the dark that hid night visits; the friend says this to turn him from secret meeting toward marriage without naming it.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field, parrots, waterfall and hill hamlet

comparisons.tenor: her bright flawless forehead
the pallor that has come over her forehead
the green ring on the small parrot's neck

193.reading: The man, giving up the journey his heart had settled on, says the road would be easy, a waste where hunters with bows leave blood on the field, a red-eared vulture feeds its young in a yaa tree and dropped flesh becomes an old jackal's meal; what he cannot do is leave the sweet sleep on the shoulders of his young wife.
193.nuance: The danger of the road is granted and then dismissed: the waste is 'easy for us'; the only hardship that counts is the bed at home. The vulture feeding its chick is the road's one image of care, and the scraps falling to the jackal show how that care spills over to others.

thinai_evidence.note: vulture, yaa tree and jackal on the hard road

comparisons.tenor: the vulture's white neck
the vulture's red ears
her smile

194.reading: The woman tells her friend that this is the very rainy season he named when he promised to come driving his chariot: rain has soaked the ploughed red furrows, the sown seed has sprouted like a spread herd of deer, and a peacock on a kurundhu branch calls like girls shooing parrots.
194.nuance: The whole description is of a working field (ploughing, weeding to the beat of a drum, the varagu harvest), so the season is fixed by labour as much as by rain; the peacock's call, compared to girls' shouts in the millet field, is the only sound, and it calls no one home.

thinai_evidence.note: the promised rains, varagu fields and kurundhu

comparisons.tenor: the red ridges of the deep furrows
the sprouting seed scattered over the field
the peacock's calls

195.reading: The mother says the other mother will gladly paint her walls and spread sand for the return of her son with the girl, while she herself, who combed the girl's hair and carried her on her hip, asks the diviner with his staff and his molucca beads whether the youth will bring the girl first to her house or take her straight to his own.
195.nuance: Her claim is not on the youth's love but on her own care for the girl; she knows she has no right to his kindness (அருளான் ஆயினும்) and asks only for a sight of her daughter. The velan is called here not to cure lovesickness but to read the eloped pair's road home.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has crossed the hard road with the youth

comparisons.tenor: the girl's gaze

196.reading: The wife tells the man of the town, where women at dawn bring hot rice and cane fruit on lily leaves to husbands asleep after eating varaal fish and drinking, that he must not come near or touch her, since his chest has embraced the woman fit for him who walks as proud as Anni Minjili after Thithiyan killed the Kosar.
196.nuance: The comparison is barbed: Anni Minjili's pride was won by revenge for her father's blinding, so the rival is cast as a woman triumphant over the wife. The opening scene of men who forget their fishing after a feast while their women still feed them at dawn may be heard as the wife's own household, but the poem leaves it as the town's picture.

thinai_evidence.note: varaal fish, water-lily leaves and the lord of the town

comparisons.tenor: the rival woman, proud in her gait
the round thick slices of fish

197.reading: The friend tells the grieving woman not to despair: though her lover has crossed Kannan Ezhini's Themuthu hill, he will not stay long, for on that cold road a tusker sleeps embracing his pregnant mate while their calf climbs on and slides off him, as a small son clambers on the chest of a father who holds his wife.
197.nuance: The simile runs backwards: the human family is the vehicle and the elephants the tenor, so the man on the road is shown his own household in the beasts. The friend's comfort rests on that sight: a man who has seen it cannot linger.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend's reassurance during the man's absence across the hills

comparisons.vehicle: மடவோள் தழீஇய விறலோன் மார்பில் புன்தலைப் புதல்வன் ஊர்புஇழிந் தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the elephant calf climbing on and sliding off the tusker who embraces his pregnant mate

iraicchi.act: the tusker embraces his pregnant mate and lets their calf climb on him as they rest together
iraicchi.sense: the man who passes this family on the road will think of his wife and child and hurry home

198.reading: The man tells his heart that the girl who, trusting his words, came at midnight through the rain with her anklets hushed, embraced him while the town slept and went away, was not a mere woman of perfect virtue but surely the dread maiden who lives in the flower-filled spring on the peak called Kaviram in Aay's southern land.
198.nuance: The awe follows the union, not first sight: having held her, he still cannot think her mortal. The peacock wreathed in young cloud gives her coming its look, while the spirit of the mountain spring gives it its danger, and both images belong to the hill.

thinai_evidence.note: a midnight tryst in the hills

comparisons.tenor: the girl coming through the rain with her dark fragrant hair
the girl who came and went in the night

colophon.thurai: புணர்ந்து நீங்கியதலைமகளது போக்கு நோக்கிய தலைமகன் தன்நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

199.reading: The man tells his heart, which urges him to go for wealth like other men, that it may go, but he will not leave his wife with her bamboo-smooth shoulders, not even for riches as great as the land Narmudi Cheral won back when Nannan fell at the battle of Vakai.
199.nuance: The road is drawn as a place of failing care: the thirsty elephant mistakes falling flowers for rain, the wild dogs scatter the deer, and only the stag at sunset calls its lost herd back with a male cry. That stag is the one creature doing what the man chooses to do.

thinai_evidence.note: thirsty elephant, wild dogs and bare trees of the waste

comparisons.tenor: the white mara flowers falling from the hill trees
the wild dogs' strong teeth
the vast forest
her large cool rounded shoulders
the wealth he refuses

iraicchi.act: at sunset the stag calls with a male cry to bring back its scattered herd
iraicchi.sense: even the stag on the road gathers its own at nightfall, so the man who stays with his wife is doing what the road itself shows

200.reading: The friend, having read the girl's wish, invites the man of the shore to their fishing hamlet of thatched huts that smells of fish and is hardly a town, yet makes anyone who stays one day forget his own city; he may yoke his chariot and go by evening, but if he stays, they too will welcome him as far as their station allows.
200.nuance: The invitation is made through modesty about the village (புலால்அம் சேரி, a fish-smelling settlement) and a boast that it makes guests forget home, so the friend accepts his suit while stating the gap in rank (எம்வரை அளவையின்) that he must accept with it.

thinai_evidence.note: the fish-smelling hamlet on the sand by the sea

comparisons.tenor: the sand of the street, shining

links.note: Both Paranar poems recall Aay Eyinan falling to Minjili with birds over the field: in 208 the birds shade the dead hero from the sun with their wings, in 181 a great flock dances thick in the sky and hides the sun's heat as he falls.
links.teaches: Read with 208, the bird flock in 181 is the known sign of Eyinan's death, the birds' honour to a fallen giver, so Paranar can use that public story as a mere measure of how thickly the Kaveri heaps its sand.

links.note: 262 tells the story of Anni Minjili, who refused food and white clothes after the Kosar blinded her father and was satisfied only when Thithiyan killed them; 196 names her in one line as the measure of the rival's gait.
links.teaches: 262 shows Anni Minjili's revenge as the lover's own surge of joy, while 196 turns the same woman into the wife's bitter picture of a triumphant rival, so one puram story served akam poets for opposite feelings.

links.note: Both Paranar marutham poems use Pazhaiyan, the Chola's warrior, lord of Por on the Kaveri: in 186 his town is the image of bangles never broken, in 326 his thrown spear is the image of a girl's eyes that never miss.
links.teaches: Together they show Paranar drawing on one patron's fame for women's power in the marutham quarrel, the fort for what holds and the spear for what strikes, so Pazhaiyan's name carried a known strength the audience could read at once.

links.note: Kural 1081 is the man's first sight: goddess, peahen or woman, his heart reels; in 198 he has already held her and still decides she is not a woman but the dread maiden of a mountain spring, having likened her coming to a peahen in cloud.
links.teaches: The couplet places the doubt at first sight and the commentators settle it in favour of a woman, but the poem keeps the same three terms after the union and settles them the other way, so the awe of the anangu was not only a first impression.

links.note: Same occasion reversed: in 182 Kapilar's friend tells the man who comes at night to come by day, for fear of the storm; in 148 Paranar's friend tells the man who comes by day to come at evening, for the girl's suffering through the long day.
links.teaches: Set side by side the two colophons show that the friend's ruling on when to meet is no fixed rule of kalavu but a reply to the present danger, and each poem names its own reason, the storm-struck night in one and the unbearable day in the other.

links.note: Both are Kayamanar's poems of the mothers left after an elopement: in 189 the foster mother wanders the house and says the town has lost its treasure; in 195 the birth mother claims her years of care and asks the diviner which house the pair will reach first.
links.teaches: Read together the two mothers' griefs differ in kind: the foster mother mourns a public loss, while the birth mother, conceding she has no claim on the youth, turns grief into a practical question about the return, which shows the elopement already moving toward an accepted marriage.

links.note: In both the man refuses a journey his heart has resolved on: in 193 he grants the road is easy and names his wife's shoulders as the one thing he cannot leave; in 199 he lets the heart go alone and refuses even a king's restored wealth.
links.teaches: Taken together the two show the refusal hardening from a weighing of costs into a full split from his own heart, and 199 adds a puram measure of the wealth refused that 193 never names.

links.note: Both are the woman telling her friend that the rainy season he promised has come without him; the colophon files 183 under paalai and 194 under mullai.
links.teaches: The pair shows the colophon thinai following different cues for one situation: 183 is labelled by the road he crossed and 194 by the fields at home, though both speak from the waiting house in the rains.

new_concepts.gloss: the appointed meeting place and time of secret lovers, by day (பகற்குறி) or by night (இரவுக்குறி)
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons of 182 and 192 (இரா வருவானைப்பகல் வர, இரவுக்குறி மறுத்தது); the verses name the night meeting

new_concepts.gloss: marriage as the end of secret love, which the friend presses the lover toward
new_concepts.label_source: ours: the tradition's term; 187, 188, 190 and 192 imply it without naming it

new_concepts.gloss: the diviner of Murugu, whom the mother consults with his molucca beads
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' word: வேலன் in 182 line 16, வேல in 195 line 14

source_issues: 183, 194: my inferred thinai (mullai for 183) differs from the colophon's paalai; both poems are the waiting wife at the arrival of the promised rains.
187: the colophon thurai gives a second alternative (…சொல்லியதூஉமாம்) without numbering the first.
189: lines 6 and 7 carry stray single quotation marks ('கவாஅன் … சுட்டிப்') that mark no speech.
192: the colophon thurai has a stray footnote numeral, 1செறிப்புஅறிவுறீஇ.
194: line 1 reads வகைறை, apparently a misprint for வைகறை.
199: line 10 reads பூளையன், apparently a misprint for பூளையின்.
190: line 17 (சேர்ந்தன்றே இலனே) is hard to construe; the reading of the rescue's end is uncertain.
183, 191: unbalanced quotation marks (183 line 1 opens a quotation that never closes; 191 line 16 closes one that never opens).
